analysis.one_liner: Writes the FTC's "click to cancel" rule into law so canceling subscriptions is as easy as signing up.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would make companies let customers cancel subscriptions as easily as they signed up, was introduced in July 2025 with 2 cosponsors and has sat in the Senate Commerce Committee since, with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would turn the FTC's "negative option" rule — known as click to cancel — into federal statute, giving it the force of law. The rule requires companies to let people cancel a subscription using the same simple steps they used to sign up, to clearly disclose the terms before charging, and to get a customer's informed consent before billing. Background: the FTC finalized this rule in 2024, but a federal appeals court blocked it just before it was due to take effect in July 2025; codifying it in statute would restore the protections and make them much harder to undo.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who pay for subscriptions — streaming services, gyms, meal kits, software, apps, newspapers — especially the many people who keep paying for services they tried to cancel or forgot to cancel. Under the rule, cancellation must be as easy as sign-up, terms must be disclosed before any charge, and companies cannot bill without informed consent, including annual reminders with a chance to opt out of renewals.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People stuck paying subscriptions they can't cancel

how_it_helps.text: Makes cancellation as easy as sign-up: a company that lets you subscribe with a few clicks or a phone call must let you cancel through the same simple route, ending the practice of hiding cancel buttons behind phone calls, chat obstacles, or in-person visits.

Requires clear disclosure of the terms before charging: companies must spell out what the product costs, how long it lasts, and what happens when a trial or promotional period ends, so people are not silently converted from free trials into paid subscriptions.

Bans billing without informed consent and requires companies to get consent before each charge, including a reminder before an annual renewal with a simple way to opt out — directly targeting revenue from forgotten, auto-renewing subscriptions.
Because the rule would be written into law rather than left as a regulation, it could not be discarded by a future administration or blocked by a court challenge the way the original rule was.

analysis.who_pays: Subscription-based businesses — streaming platforms, gyms and fitness studios, software companies, media outlets, and subscription-box sellers — which would have to rebuild their sign-up and cancellation systems and would lose revenue from customers who currently stay subscribed because canceling is hard or because they forgot a trial converted to a paid plan. Some of that cost may be passed on to consumers in the form of higher prices or fewer free trials.
analysis.who_pays_short: Streaming, gym, media, and software subscription businesses

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs are real: businesses would have to rework sign-up, cancellation, and renewal flows, keep records of consent, and send renewal reminders — a heavier lift for small publishers, gyms, and other small businesses than for large streaming platforms.

Companies would lose revenue from subscribers who would have cancelled but for the friction, or who forgot a free trial rolled into a paid plan; some of that revenue is legitimate, and businesses argue easier cancellation will mean fewer trial offers and higher prices for everyone.
The bill freezes one snapshot of the rule — Part 425 of title 16 as it stood on July 7, 2025 — into statute, which removes the FTC's flexibility to update the details as business practices change.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is small and visible: some friction-based subscription revenue moves back to consumers in exchange for compliance costs that fall hardest on small subscription businesses. The consumer-side benefit is broad — nearly every household pays subscriptions, and forgotten or trap-style renewals are a common drain — while the costs are narrower and mostly borne by businesses whose model relies on the friction. The main design weakness is that codifying a fixed July 2025 snapshot of the rule into statute makes it harder to adapt over time.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2025 and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote; Congress is still in session, so it is technically alive.

narrative.text: Senator Ruben Gallego introduced the bill on July 10, 2025, together with Senator Peter Welch.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
Two Democratic senators cosponsored it, and no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — appears in the record since the referral.

Timing matters: the bill arrived days after a federal appeals court vacated the FTC's click-to-cancel rule before it could take effect on July 14, 2025, which is why the bill's approach is to give the rule statutory force.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Subscription businesses that profit from hard-to-cancel memberships and forgotten renewals are better off so far: the underlying rule remains blocked in court, and the bill that would restore it has gone nowhere in committee.

for.name: Ruben Gallego
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill to codify the FTC's click-to-cancel rule.

for.name: Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor who joined Gallego in introducing the bill.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Republican-led in the 119th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing or markup appears in the record.

against.name: Subscription-business trade groups (including the National Federation of Independent Business and the Interactive Advertising Bureau)
against.role: Industry opponents of the underlying FTC rule
against.what_they_did: Challenged the FTC's click-to-cancel rule in federal court, where it was vacated before taking effect, and lobbied against it.

sides.party_line_note: All three senators behind the bill are Democrats (the sponsor and two cosponsors), there are no Republican cosponsors, and the bill sits in the Senate committee led by Republicans with no scheduled action.

industries.industry: Subscription businesses (streaming, gyms, media, apps, subscription boxes)
industries.note: The rule these companies would have to follow bars them from making cancellation harder than sign-up and requires informed consent and renewal reminders. Many rely on retention friction and forgotten auto-renewals for a meaningful share of revenue, so the bill directly transfers that revenue back to subscribers.

Businesses built on converting free trials into paid plans without customers noticing would have to disclose terms up front and get consent before charging, cutting off a common dark-pattern sales funnel.

analysis.trajectory: A Senate bill with one-party sponsorship, no committee hearing, and no movement in its first months rarely advances; with Republicans controlling the Senate floor agenda, the most likely path is that it never gets a vote and dies at the end of this Congress, though consumer-protection language like this occasionally gets folded into a larger package.
